01

Start here

The reasoning frame

What is happening now?→ Need rapid bronchodilation?→ Need inflammation control?→ How severe / how controlled?→ Which add-on fits phenotype?

Acute symptoms: think bronchodilator first. Persistent disease: anchor the long-term plan with inhaled corticosteroid. Failure despite optimized therapy: step up, check adherence/technique, then consider LAMA, phenotype-matched biologics, or systemic steroids at the most severe end.

Professor-level core rule: the drug that makes the airway feel open is not automatically treating the disease process. A LABA can improve symptoms while inflammation continues, which is why asthma LABA therapy must remain paired with ICS.

Exam sheet

Part I — Core framework and must-know content

1) The whole lecture in one map

Bronchoconstriction now→SABA ± SAMA →Persistent inflammation→ICS backbone →Still uncontrolled→ICS/LABA → higher ICS dose → LAMA/biologic
Must know: LABA/uLABA never as monotherapy in asthma. The long-acting bronchodilator can mask symptoms while inflammation continues. Pair with ICS.

2) Bronchodilators

DrugMechanismRoleKey toxicity / trap
Albuterolβ2 → Gs → AC → ↑cAMP/PKA → relaxationRapid rescue; acute exacerbationTachycardia, tremor, anxiety, weakness, hypokalemia; not drowsiness
FormoterolSame β2 pathwayLABA adjunct; rapid onset allows ICS-formoterol reliever/SMARTNever alone in asthma
Vilanterolβ2 agonist~24 h maintenance; asthma only with ICSDo not remove ICS and leave uLABA alone
IpratropiumCompetitive muscarinic blockAcute adjunct to albuterol; DuoNebDry mouth, glaucoma/urinary retention concern
TiotropiumLong-acting muscarinic blockHigher-step maintenance add-onNot first-line mild-asthma controller
TheophyllinePDE inhibition ↑cAMP + adenosine antagonism + HDAC effectRare severe-asthma adjunctNarrow window, CYP1A2 interactions, vomiting, arrhythmias, seizures, death

4) Stepwise treatment logic

  • Initial choice = classify severity. Use impairment + risk: symptoms, night waking, reliever frequency, activity, spirometry, exacerbation history/severity.
  • Follow-up adjustment = assess control. Well controlled → maintain/consider step-down after sustained control; not well controlled → step up; very poorly controlled → larger step-up and consider steroid burst.
  • ICS is the backbone. It is the main drug class whose controller dose is adjusted upward/downward.
  • Preferred adjunct: LABA, always paired with ICS. At higher steps consider LAMA and phenotype-specific biologics.
  • Step down one medication at a time. Do not reflexively step down right before a patient’s predictable bad season.

5) GINA / SMART lecture emphasis

ICS-formoterol can serve as both maintenance and reliever therapy because formoterol has rapid onset and each symptom-driven puff also delivers anti-inflammatory ICS. The lecture’s GINA 2026 framework begins as-needed ICS-formoterol at early steps, then daily + PRN use at higher steps. Per the lecture, U.S. rescue use is not FDA-approved and insurance quantity/coverage can be a barrier.

Professor-emphasized traps

Trap Fluticasone is not a direct bronchodilator. It reduces future bronchoconstriction by controlling inflammation.
Trap Drowsiness is not an albuterol adverse effect. Think jittery/anxious/tremulous + tachycardia/hypokalemia.
Trap Ipratropium supports albuterol acutely. It does not replace the SABA as the main initial bronchodilator in the lecture.
Trap Do not dose-escalate the LABA as the step-up lever. The lecture emphasizes ICS dose adjustment.
Nuance A good regimen the patient will not take is not a good regimen. The lecturer explicitly emphasized adherence, patient preference, and insurance feasibility.
Nuance The lecture sources use slightly different steroid-burst wording: the controller summary cites roughly 4–10 days, while cases/transcript often describe ~3–5 or 5 days. Know the course concept rather than treating one duration as the only lecture value.

Sources and clarifications

Materials used

  • 9-28-2026_Kramer_Drugs_for_Asthma (3).pptx — 98-slide lecture deck.
  • Drugs for Asthma-transcript (1).txt — professor emphasis, causal explanations, clinical preferences, and nuance.
  • 9-28-2026_Kramer_Drugs_for_Asthma_Objectives.V1 (2).docx — required drug list and learning objectives.
  • Drugs_for_Asthma_-_Practice_Questions.docx — four professor-provided questions/answer key used as practice anchors.
  • study guide html … formatting update.docx — Learning Lab design/delivery requirements.

Lecture-specific clarifications

  • The lecture intentionally teaches both the older NIH/NHLBI stepwise framework and the professor’s current GINA 2026 emphasis. This guide preserves that distinction instead of silently merging them.
  • The lecture states that ICS-formoterol reliever/SMART use is not FDA-approved in the U.S. and may face insurance coverage/quantity barriers. That is preserved as a course point.
  • Systemic steroid burst duration is expressed differently across the lecture materials (short 3–5/5-day case wording vs a 4–10-day summary range). The exam sheet flags this rather than inventing a single “corrected” duration.
  • No broad board-review material was added when it would displace lecture-specific drug selection, mechanisms, or professor-tested distinctions.

Built as a self-contained offline HTML file. Practice questions deliberately hide source/provenance until submission.
